p4c1.essay:
Part Three ended inside a nightmare, with a stranger in the doorway and a fly buzzing against the pane ([[p3c6]]). Part Four opens on the same breath: 'Can this be still a dream?' Dostoevsky does not let that question close for a long while, and I think it is the first thing to notice about Svidrigaïlov. He has been a name in the book since the mother's letter in [[p1c3]], the lecherous landowner of a provincial scandal, and everyone, the reader included, has a villain ready for him. The man who actually sits down is something else: affable, well-bred, impossible to insult, and funny. Raskolnikov shows him the door almost at once, and he laughs 'in the frankest way' and stays for the whole chapter.

It took me more than one reading to see how the conversation is built. Raskolnikov starts as the examiner, firing rude questions, and Svidrigaïlov answers every one without flinching: yes, he struck his wife 'just twice with a switch'; yes, he was a card-sharper; yes, he was bought out of a debtors' prison and kept on a leash for seven years. That candour is the unsettling thing. He excuses himself the way a man tidies a room, without urgency, and his excuses have a horrible plausibility because they are built from observations the novel has already made in earnest. That people 'greatly love to be insulted' is a foul thing to say about a dead wife; it is also a fair description of Marmeladov. And somewhere in the middle the examination reverses. Raskolnikov, who has spent three parts being told he is ill, hears himself say 'You should go to a doctor.' For once he is the sane one in the room, and he does not enjoy it.

The reversal comes with the ghosts. Svidrigaïlov sees his dead wife, and what I love about these visitations is how unghostly they are. Marfa Petrovna reminds him to wind the dining-room clock. She offers to tell his fortune. She shows off a green silk dress and scolds him about remarrying. No message from beyond, no accusation, just the marriage continuing after the funeral, nagging and all. A lesser writer would have sent her to point a finger. Dostoevsky sends her to talk 'the silliest trifles', and the effect is far worse, because it suggests that what follows death might be exactly as small as what came before it. Which is where Svidrigaïlov goes next: eternity not as something vast but as 'one little room, like a bath house in the country', black and grimy, with spiders in the corners. I find this the most frightening paragraph in the novel so far, more than the axe, and the reason is the tone. He is not trying to shock. He adds, 'with a vague smile', that it is what he would have made it himself. Raskolnikov cries out for something 'juster and more comforting', and that cry is worth pausing on, coming from a man who has just said flatly that he does not believe in a future life.

Then there is the claim that keeps surfacing, each time more openly: 'something in common between us', 'Here's the man', 'birds of a feather'. Raskolnikov denies it with a heat that gives him away, and he has already half conceded it by blurting out that he somehow expected the ghosts. What is the common thing? Svidrigaïlov does not say and claims not to know. I would not hurry to decide. The safe observation is that each of them is a man alone in a room with something he has done, and that Svidrigaïlov has no theory about it at all. Raskolnikov needed an article and a Napoleon in order to step over; this man shrugs and says 'Reason is the slave of passion.' If Raskolnikov's idea were stripped of its justifications and left to grow old and bored, it might look like this. That is my reading, and the chapter is careful not to confirm it.

Finally, the business. He wants to give Dounia ten thousand roubles, no conditions, 'to show that I am not, after all, privileged to do nothing but harm'. I believe that sentence and distrust the offer, both at once, and I think Dostoevsky wants exactly that double response. Notice also what slips out sideways: a 'journey' he mentions and then seems to forget, a balloon, a possible bride, and the remark that he was struck by Raskolnikov's face 'this morning'. He has been watching. He leaves saying he is staying very near.

annotations.quote: human beings in general, indeed, greatly love to be insulted, have you noticed that?
annotations.note: A vile generalisation, offered as small talk. The trouble is that the novel has already supplied the evidence: think of Marmeladov calling it a consolation to be dragged by the hair in [[p1c2]]. Svidrigaïlov's cynicism tends to be made of true observations put to bad use.

annotations.quote: in those days of beneficent publicity
annotations.note: Garnett's 'publicity' is glasnost, the catchword of the early 1860s, when a newly loosened press took to exposing private misbehaviour. The 'disgraceful action of the Age' was a real row of 1861: a newspaper sneered at a lady who had read Cleopatra's lines from Pushkin's 'Egyptian Nights' in public. Svidrigaïlov remembers the reform years the way a man remembers a season at the theatre, chiefly for 'the dark eyes'.

annotations.quote: bought me off for thirty thousand silver pieces
annotations.note: Dostoevsky uses the biblical word here, the one for Judas's pieces of silver, and Garnett keeps a trace of it before switching to 'roubles' a line later. The joke is turned inside out, since he is the one who was bought. Seven years with the IOU held over him, and he insists it was not the document that kept him.

annotations.quote: What’s most revolting is that one is really sad!
annotations.note: The Bay of Naples makes him sad, and the insult is that the sadness is genuine, not a pose he could laugh off. Under the chatter this is the man's real complaint: nothing interests him and he knows it. Count how often he says he is bored.

annotations.quote: She comes, speaks to me for a minute and goes out at the door--always at the door.
annotations.note: His ghost keeps house rules: she uses the door. That domestic detail is what makes the story hard to dismiss as something told for effect. It comes minutes after Raskolnikov woke from his own dream of the old woman in [[p3c6]] to find this man standing in his doorway.

annotations.quote: What made me think that something of the sort must be happening to you?
annotations.note: The most surprising line in the chapter, and it surprises its speaker. He has spent the scene holding this man at arm's length, and here he admits he had guessed at him from the inside. Svidrigaïlov pounces at once.

annotations.quote: I don’t believe in a future life
annotations.note: Compare [[p3c5]], where Porfiry asked whether he believed in God and in the raising of Lazarus and he said yes, literally. Either he was lying then, or he is lying now, or, as I suspect, he does not know. The denial does not stop him demanding, a few lines on, that eternity be just.

annotations.quote: what if it’s one little room, like a bath house in the country, black and grimy and spiders in every corner
annotations.note: Not hellfire and not nothing, but a small dirty outbuilding that goes on for ever. In Russian folk belief the village bath house was the unclean corner of the homestead, the one building where no icon hung. An eternity without grandeur is a more modern terror than damnation, and he delivers it conversationally.

annotations.quote: to show that I am not, after all, privileged to do nothing but harm
annotations.note: The sentence I can't get past. It is a strange thing for a cynic to want, and stranger to say to a hostile young man he met half an hour ago. His logic afterwards is uncomfortably good: in marrying Luzhin, Dounia 'is taking money just the same, only from another man'.

annotations.quote: if only you knew what you are asking
annotations.note: The 'journey' comes up more than once and each time he swerves away from it: to a balloon, to a marriage, to a short loud laugh. He plainly means more by the word than he says. Hold on to it.

links.why: The nightmare this chapter wakes out of; read its last page again and the opening question here stops being a figure of speech.
The mother's letter, where Svidrigaïlov was first described; set that provincial villain beside the man who actually turns up.
Raskolnikov tells Porfiry he believes in God and in Lazarus, and defends his theory of those who may step over; both look different after an hour with Svidrigaïlov.
He says he was struck by Raskolnikov's face 'this morning'; it is worth rereading who was out in the street that morning, and who was noticed by whom.

p4c2.essay:
After the bath house, a tea table. The chapter is a comedy of manners, and it should be read hard on the heels of [[p4c1]] to feel how deliberately Dostoevsky has set the two side by side. We have just listened to Svidrigaïlov on himself; now we get Svidrigaïlov according to Luzhin, a dossier of the worst available rumours delivered with 'I have precise information.' A deaf and dumb girl found hanging, a servant driven to his death. These are dreadful stories and the book gives us no means of checking them. What it gives instead is the teller, a man we know slanders for advantage, and Dounia's dry correction, which comes from someone who actually lived in that house. I notice that she, of all people, is the one who insists on fairness to Svidrigaïlov, and that Luzhin at once tries to make something dirty of it.

Then the trial. Dounia has set the evening up as a test, 'you or he', and she means to judge honestly; she even promises that Rodya will apologise if he is in the wrong. Luzhin could pass with one generous sentence. Instead he hears being weighed against a brother as an affront to his rank, and every reply digs him deeper, 'as though he relished it'. What finishes him is not Raskolnikov's contempt but the three thousand roubles. The moment the legacy is announced he remarks that the ladies' new tone is 'very apropos', which is to confess that the engagement rested on their having nowhere else to go. Raskolnikov worked that out from a letter back in [[p1c4]]; here Luzhin proves it out of his own mouth, and caps it with 'expenses'. Pulcheria Alexandrovna's answer about the trunk is the best line the poor woman has had.

Two quieter things. Luzhin, lecturing on insults, says there is a line it is dangerous to overstep, and no return once it is overstepped. He means manners, but that verb is the novel's title, and Raskolnikov is sitting three feet away. And Raskolnikov himself is oddly absent from his own victory. On the way over he asks Razumihin twice whether he really saw the visitor, and he thinks, about his friend, 'what will you say to-morrow?' Something has been decided offstage, and the tea party is taking place in front of it.

annotations.quote: I keep thinking that it may have been an hallucination
annotations.note: He has good reason to ask. The visitor arrived on the tail of a nightmare, talked about ghosts, and nobody else was in the room. Razumihin's 'I should know him in a thousand' is the only outside confirmation the reader gets, too.

annotations.quote: it had never occurred to him to wonder what Razumihin would think when he knew
annotations.note: 'When', not 'if'. Tucked inside a paragraph about Razumihin's bluster is the news that Raskolnikov has some intention for tomorrow. The narrator moves straight on to tea.

annotations.quote: become more like sacks of flour than elegant and lively men of society
annotations.note: Dostoevsky's comic gift is underrated. Luzhin depends on a script; cross him and the elegance has nothing behind it. The cambric handkerchief 'reeking of scent' a few paragraphs earlier is the same joke told with a prop.

annotations.quote: he hanged himself partly on account of Mr. Svidrigaïlov’s mockery of him and not his blows
annotations.note: This Philip is the Filka whose ghost came for a pipe in [[p4c1]], where the story was only 'a violent quarrel just before his death'. That makes three versions: Svidrigaïlov's, Luzhin's, and Dounia's, the only one from somebody with nothing to gain. In hers the weapon was mockery.

annotations.quote: There is a line in everything which it is dangerous to overstep
annotations.note: Luzhin means etiquette. But the Russian word for 'crime' in the title is literally a stepping-over, and Raskolnikov's article in [[p3c5]] was about who is entitled to do it. The pompous fiancé states the law of the book without knowing it, to the one man at the table it concerns.

annotations.quote: For your sake I must break off with my brother, for my brother’s sake I must break off with you.
annotations.note: Dounia is the clearest head in the room. She frames a symmetrical test and binds herself to the result before it starts. It is the family absolutism put to honest use: like her brother she wants to know 'for certain', but she asks out loud.

annotations.quote: in the presence of Mr. Razsudkin
annotations.note: A calculated slip. Razumihin's name is built on the Russian word for reason, and Luzhin swaps in a near-synonym, something like 'Mr. Commonsense'. Petty, and of a piece with the polite bow that goes with it.

annotations.quote: when the news has come of Marfa Petrovna’s legacy, which seems indeed very apropos
annotations.note: Here he gives the game away. Only a man who had been counting on their poverty would notice so quickly that it has ended. Dounia catches it in the very next line.

annotations.quote: I have been led on account of that into expenses
annotations.note: The word Raskolnikov laughs at, and rightly: at the moment of losing the woman he says he adores, Luzhin reaches for the ledger. The expense in question turns out to be a trunk that travelled free.

annotations.quote: Him, and him alone, he blamed for everything.
annotations.note: Luzhin cannot blame the women without admitting that they judged him, so the whole weight falls on the brother. The narrator stops to tell us this hatred is of a rare size. I would not forget it.

links.why: Luzhin's letter in full, with the 'urgent request' that Raskolnikov be kept away and the slander about the money given to the widow.
The first meeting in the garret, where Raskolnikov threw the theory of the poor and grateful bride back in Luzhin's face; this is the insult being litigated at the tea table.
Svidrigaïlov's own account of his wife, his serf Filka and his money, heard an hour and a half before Luzhin's version.
Raskolnikov's furious reading of his mother's letter, where he first saw what kind of bargain this marriage was.

p4c3.essay:
The chapter opens with something Dostoevsky rarely allows himself in this book: several minutes inside a head that is not Raskolnikov's. Luzhin on the stairs is a small masterpiece of contempt. The parenthesis '(she must be poor)' does more than a page of denunciation could, and so does the detail that he honestly regards taking Dounia as 'heroic' while knowing perfectly well the gossip about her was false. He is sincere, which is what makes him unbearable. I am struck too that his daydream is about gratitude rather than desire: a wife who will 'humble herself in the dust' for life. Set that beside what Svidrigaïlov proposed in [[p4c1]], money with nothing asked in return, and the respectable suitor comes off worse than the libertine. I don't think that is an accident, though I would not trust either man.

Then the row of asterisks, and the mood turns right over. For a couple of pages this is the happiest the book has been. There is money that came honestly, a friend who is transparently in love and has a business plan, a flat in the same house, work that Raskolnikov is actually fitted for. Razumihin's scheme is no fantasy; Dostoevsky had run journals himself and knew the trade from inside, and he lets Raskolnikov be drawn in, almost against his will, as far as 'I know of one book myself.' Everything his poverty was supposed to explain is being handed back to him across a tea table. The idea he overheard in [[p1c6]] ran on arithmetic, one life against all the good that money could do. Here are the means without the murder, a week too late, and he picks up his cap.

That is why the leave-taking hurts as it does. Nobody drives him out. He walks away from the one room in Petersburg where he is loved, and tells them that if they hold on to him he will begin to hate them. I believe him, and I don't read it as coldness. Their affection is addressed to a person he can no longer pretend to be, and every kind word lands on someone else.

And then the corridor, the lamp, the long look. 'Some idea, some hint' passes, 'awful, hideous, and suddenly understood on both sides.' Dostoevsky will not say what, and I would resist filling in the blank too confidently; a look is not a confession, and the narrator hurries past at once with 'I will not attempt to describe.' What is certain is the errand. He has just handed his family over to Razumihin, and Razumihin has accepted.

annotations.quote: sometimes even gloated in solitude over his image in the glass
annotations.note: A man who made his own way and admires the result in private. Dostoevsky is merciless but exact: this is the vanity of someone who was once nobody and has only his money to prove otherwise.

annotations.quote: virtuous, poor (she must be poor), very young, very pretty
annotations.note: Four words in brackets and the whole man is there. The poverty is not an obstacle he is willing to overlook; it is the requirement. Compare the theory of the grateful wife as Raskolnikov flung it back at him in [[p2c5]].

annotations.quote: He had only been a tiny bit masterful, had not even time to speak out, had simply made a joke
annotations.note: The narration has slid into Luzhin's own voice; these are his excuses, in his vocabulary, with the quotation marks taken off. Garnett's 'a tiny bit masterful' catches the wheedling tone nicely.

annotations.quote: Pulcheria Alexandrovna was surprised to find that she, too, was glad
annotations.note: A lovely small truth. That morning the break would have been a catastrophe; now it is a relief she had not let herself want. The three thousand roubles help, and Dostoevsky says so more than once without sneering at her.

annotations.quote: He says he is going away, and in ten minutes he forgets he has said it.
annotations.note: Raskolnikov's summary is accurate and leaves out the ghosts, the bath house and 'birds of a feather'. He reports the business and keeps back everything that touched him.

annotations.quote: He had told a lie then, and Raskolnikov knew he was lying.
annotations.note: In [[p2c2]] Razumihin pleaded weak German so that his starving friend would take half the work and half the fee. Only now does the narrator tell us it was a lie and that Raskolnikov saw through it. A kindness on one side, and on the other a man who noticed it and still walked out.

annotations.quote: You need not be a saint to make pots, believe me!
annotations.note: A Russian proverb, more usually put as 'it is not gods who fire the pots': ordinary people can learn a trade. Garnett's 'saint' softens it a little. It is Razumihin's whole creed, and the reverse of dividing mankind into the ordinary and the extraordinary.

annotations.quote: One would think you were burying me or saying good-bye for ever
annotations.note: He reaches for a joke and says what he is thinking instead; the narrator underlines it with 'it somehow was uttered aloud.' This keeps happening to him, as with the blurted question about ghosts in [[p4c1]].

annotations.quote: now if you love me, give me up... else I shall begin to hate you, I feel it
annotations.note: I take this literally. Love that begs him to be 'as before' is asking for someone who no longer exists, and he can feel what that pressure will turn into. It is the most honest thing he says to them.

annotations.quote: Razumihin remembered that minute all his life.
annotations.note: A sudden long view: for one clause the narrator stands years beyond this corridor. It gives nothing away about what is to come, only that for Razumihin this was the minute that counted.

links.why: The translation job and the 'schwach' German: Razumihin's first attempt to share his work with Raskolnikov, refused on the stairs.
The overheard tavern argument that one death could be paid for by the good done with the money; read it beside a table where money and work are simply offered.
The family's first reunion, where he already felt he could never again speak freely to them; this farewell finishes what that scene began.
He walks out of this house with 'sharp determination'; the next chapter shows where he was going.
